source.title: EfficientLLM: Scalable Pruning-Aware Pretraining for Architecture-Agnostic Edge Language Models
source.authors: Xing-Run Xing; Zheng Liu; Shitao Xiao; Bo-Yan Gao; Yi-Ming Liang; Wan-Peng Zhang; Hao-Kun Lin; Guo-Qi Li; Jia-Jun Zhang

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports downstream benchmark results while scaling continued pretraining in the new setting of pruning-aware pretraining; it does not reproduce the original held-out-loss scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper discusses scaling laws and claims its approach exceeds the traditional parameter scaling law, but does not fit power laws to held-out cross-entropy loss, test extrapolation from small runs, or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. The relevant results are downstream benchmark scores for EfficientLLM-A at different continued-pretraining token counts, plus a figure described as showing improved pruning performance with more pruning data.
record.test_reason: An edge-model pruning paper. It invokes Kaplan et al. as motivation and asserts it 'exceeds the traditional LLM scaling law' by comparing benchmark scores of different models. It fits no power law, reports no held-out loss, and runs no predictive test. The only scale contrasts are two-point continued-pretraining token comparisons of its own EfficientLLM-A models, plus Fig. 5 on pruning-token amount. These report its own method's performance and cannot show predictable scaling, so they do not test V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling structural pruning into pretraining yields edge models (100M–1.1B) that beat direct-pretraining and post-training-pruning baselines on benchmarks. Their claim to 'exceed the traditional LLM scaling law' rests on cross-model benchmark comparisons at smaller data budgets, not on any loss fit or scaling-law measurement.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses saliency-driven structural pruning during pretraining and reports downstream benchmark scores; it does not use the original scaling-law procedure of fitting held-out-loss curves over parameter, token, or compute sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says pruning-aware pretraining token requirements depend on iterations to reach the target parameter count and can be adjusted through batch size and pruning frequency. It also varies pruning-to-gradient-step ratios in the scalability experiment, but the text does not give outcome values by ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: For EfficientLLM-A, average commonsense accuracy rises with more continued pretraining tokens: 54.77 to 57.35 at 469M, and 59.03 to 60.75 at 1.1B. Fig. 5 is described as showing that more pruning-aware tokens improve pruned-model accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For pruned-from-larger small models, downstream accuracy keeps improving with more continued or pruning-aware pretraining tokens.

record.problems: No held-out cross-entropy results or scaling-law fits are reported. The downstream comparisons use selected token-count points, provide no uncertainty estimates, and do not establish a predictive curve. The Figure 5 trend is described in text but its values are not stated.

untested.parts: No held-out loss and no power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits extrapolated to larger runs.
Architectures are compared in Tables 5–6, but with no controlled loss comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or regime with power-law fits.
No fit or prediction of downstream scores from scale or loss; only two token points per model of its own method.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' and 'limits_scope' labels are dropped. Two-point token comparisons of the study's own method cannot show predictable downstream scaling, and the claimed decreases (r12, r17) are negligible. Table 2 lists 320B tokens for the 1.1B model, while Table 7 lists 50B/500B; this inconsistency is noted.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy loss measurements or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions compared with much larger runs.
No fixed-compute budget sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No controlled comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities, repeated-data regimes, or fine-tuning/transfer power-law measurements.

Reports downstream benchmark scores at selected token counts, but does not fit or validate a predictive relationship, measure pretraining loss, or test downstream predictability across several orders of magnitude.
No comparison of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits across fitting choices, and no test for curves bending away from a single power law.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: EfficientLLM-A at 469M and 1.1B; reported aggregate scores and most task metrics at the compared continued-pretraining token counts
reader_labels.reason: Reported average benchmark accuracy rises with more continued-pretraining tokens in both comparisons, and most individual task scores rise as well (r01–r10, r13–r16, r18–r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: These scores decrease slightly at the higher continued-pretraining token count, so the increase is not consistent across every reported task metric (r12, r17).
